title: Mac and Cheese
subtitle: baked pasta in a rich cheese sauce
excerpt: A proper baked mac and cheese with a smooth, creamy sauce and a golden top. It uses a simple roux base with lots of cheddar and a hit of black pepper. This is comfort food at its most straightforward.
sourceNotes: Baked macaroni and cheese has been a fixture of American cooking since Thomas Jefferson reportedly served it at a White House dinner in 1802. The dish became a family staple through the 20th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the sauce ahead and refrigerate. Cook fresh pasta before baking.

content.text: Cook the pasta two minutes short of the packet time. It will finish cooking in the oven and you do not want it to go mushy. Keep the sauce loose before baking -- it thickens as it heats.

items.prepNote: use 250g mature cheddar, grated -- plus extra for topping

content.text: Preheat the oven to 180C (fan 160C / gas 4). Cook the pasta in salted boiling water for 2 minutes less than the packet says. Drain and set aside.
Melt the butter in the empty saucepan over medium heat. Add the flour and whisk for 1 minute to make a roux.
Pour in the milk gradually, whisking constantly after each addition. Keep whisking until the sauce is smooth.
Bring the sauce to a simmer, whisking, until it thickens -- about 5 minutes. Season with salt and black pepper.
Remove from heat. Stir in two-thirds of the cheese until melted and smooth.
Stir the cooked pasta into the cheese sauce. Transfer to a baking dish.
Scatter the remaining cheese over the top. Bake for 20 minutes until golden and bubbling.

items.cause: Milk added too fast without whisking
items.fix: Add the milk a small amount at a time and whisk vigorously between additions. Warm the milk slightly before adding if lumps persist.

items.cause: Pasta cooked to full time before baking
items.fix: Always undercook the pasta by 2 minutes. It absorbs liquid and softens further in the oven.

items.cause: Heat too high when melting the cheese
items.fix: Remove the sauce from the heat before stirring in the cheese. High heat can cause it to separate.

content.text: Mac and cheese is woven into American food culture at every level. A version appeared in American cookbooks as early as the 1820s. It became a household staple through the 20th century, particularly in the American South where baked versions are a fixture at family gatherings. Today it is eaten everywhere from school canteens to upmarket restaurants.
